newsitem.title: UK: No sign of crisis in Iraq - British sources.
newsitem.headline: No sign of crisis in Iraq - British sources.

text.p: There is no sign of an impending crisis or any unusual military activity in Iraq despite "colourful" U.S. claims of a power struggle there, British sources said on Thursday.
"Things continue as normal. We have no heightened alert status," said one British offical on condition of anonymity.

"I can't see any sign that anything too dramatic is actually happening. There is no sign of any special military preparations or anything of that kind. They exercise like any other armed forces. There is no sign of any impending crisis."
His remarks came one day after senior U.S. officials branded Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein a "demon" and said there were signs of a power struggle in Baghdad.

A senior U.S. military source had earlier painted a picture of dramatic upheaval in Saddam's inner circle, saying the Iraqi leader had put his wife under house arrest and was changing locations more frequently out of apparent fear for his safety.

The senior military officer had summoned reporters on Tuesday to say that various sources he considered reliable reported signs of increasing trouble surrounding Saddam, a bitter foe of the United States since U.S.-led forces ousted Iraqi invaders from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.

Besides the reported house arrest of Saddam's wife, the military officer said the Iraqi ruler's eldest son and heir apparent, Uday, might lose a leg to gangrene as a result of a December 12 grenade and machine-gun attack in Baghdad.
An Iraqi government spokesman ridiculed the U.S. statements as a "distortion and propaganda ploy against Iraq".
Iraqi dissidents said the recent U.S. statements gave an accurate account of rifts in Saddam's ruling circle.

They said Washington's tough talk was meant to send a clear message from newly installed Clinton administration officials to Western allies and people inside Iraq that Saddam must go before any thaw in relations with Baghdad.
But the British sources disputed much of the U.S. military official's account, saying life appeared to continue as normal in Iraq.
Britain does not know how badly Saddam's son Uday was injured when he was attacked but "we have seen nothing to suggest he has gangrene or anything like that," said one source.
Nor did Britain have any information to back up the U.S. suggestion that Saddam had placed his wife under house arrest, he said.
